description: Original short practice and find-the-mistake examples for six UK A-level textbook companion pages. These are not official Edexcel questions and do not constitute a full syllabus diagnostic.
math_format: LaTeX with inline \( ... \) and display \[ ... \] delimiters
timing_note: Suggested time applies to the three core questions in each book. The find-the-mistake question is an optional extension.

pure-year-1.title: Pure Mathematics Year 1
pure-year-1.intro: Three short checks on inequalities, stationary points and definite integration. Show enough working to make your method clear.

questions.hint: Factorise, then decide where the upward-opening quadratic is on or below the horizontal axis.
solution: Factorising gives \(x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\), so the roots are \(2\) and \(3\).
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is positive, so the graph is below the axis between the roots. Equality is allowed, so both endpoints are included.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\), find the coordinates of both stationary points and classify each one.
questions.hint: Solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=0\), substitute back into \(f\), then use the sign of \(f^{\prime\prime}\).
solution: \(f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)\), so the stationary points occur at \(x=1\) and \(x=3\).
\(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x-12\). Since \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)=-6<0\), \((1,5)\) is a local maximum. Since \(f^{\prime\prime}(3)=6>0\), \((3,1)\) is a local minimum.

questions.hint: Find an antiderivative and subtract its value at the lower limit from its value at the upper limit.
solution: An antiderivative of \(2x+1\) is \(x^2+x\).

mistake.prompt: A student writes \(\sqrt{(x-2)^2}=x-2\) for every real \(x\). Explain the error and give a statement that is always correct.
mistake.hint: The square-root symbol denotes the non-negative square root. Test a value less than \(2\).
solution: At \(x=0\), the left side is \(\sqrt{4}=2\), whereas the claimed right side is \(-2\). Squaring removes a sign, so taking the non-negative square root does not always recover the original expression.
The correct identity is \(\sqrt{(x-2)^2}=|x-2|\). This equals \(x-2\) when \(x\geq 2\), and \(2-x\) when \(x<2\).

recommendations: Pair quadratic factorisation with a quick sketch, then practise choosing intervals for both strict and inclusive inequalities.
For stationary-point questions, finish the full chain: derivative, roots, coordinates and classification.
After practising one method, try a mixed exercise without looking at its chapter heading. Explain how you chose the method.

pure-year-2.title: Pure Mathematics Year 2
pure-year-2.intro: Three short checks on trigonometric equations, parametric tangents and integration by parts. Angles are in radians.

questions.hint: Treat \(\sin x\) as the variable while factorising, then find every angle in the stated interval.
solution: \(2\sin^2x+\sin x-1=(2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)\). Hence \(\sin x=\tfrac12\) or \(\sin x=-1\).
In the given interval, \(\sin x=\tfrac12\) gives \(x=\tfrac\pi6\) and \(x=\tfrac{5\pi}6\). The equation \(\sin x=-1\) gives \(x=\tfrac{3\pi}2\).

questions.prompt: A curve is given by \(x=t^2+1\), \(y=t^3-3t\). Find the equation of its tangent at \(t=2\).
questions.hint: Use \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x=(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t)/(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t)\), and find the point as well as the gradient.
solution: At \(t=2\), \(x=5\) and \(y=2\), so the required point is \((5,2)\).
\(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t=2t\) and \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t=3t^2-3\). Thus \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x=(3t^2-3)/(2t)\), which is \(9/4\) at \(t=2\).
The tangent through \((5,2)\) with gradient \(9/4\) is \(y-2=\tfrac94(x-5)\).

questions.hint: In integration by parts, differentiate \(x\) and integrate \(e^x\).
solution: Take \(u=x\) and \(\mathrm{d}v=e^x\,\mathrm{d}x\), so \(\mathrm{d}u=\mathrm{d}x\) and \(v=e^x\).
\[\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 xe^x\,\mathrm{d}x&=[xe^x]_0^1-\int_0^1e^x\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=e-(e-1)=1.\end{aligned}\]

mistake.prompt: A student calculates \(\int_{-1}^1x\,\mathrm{d}x=0\) and concludes that the total area between \(y=x\) and the horizontal axis on this interval is zero. Correct the conclusion.
mistake.hint: Sketch the line. Contributions to a definite integral can cancel even when geometric areas are positive.
solution: The integral is correctly calculated as zero: the contribution below the axis is \(-1/2\) and the contribution above the axis is \(1/2\).
Total area adds their magnitudes. Equivalently, \(\int_{-1}^1|x|\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\).
mistake.answer: The signed integral is \(0\); the total area is \(1\) square unit.

recommendations: Keep the interval and angle units visible when solving trigonometric equations; use a sketch to check for missing roots.
Before integrating, decide whether simplification, substitution or integration by parts makes the structure easier.
Use graph sketches to check signs, turning points and cancellation before committing to lengthy algebra.

statistics-mechanics-year-1.title: Statistics and Mechanics Year 1
statistics-mechanics-year-1.intro: Three short checks on probability, coded data and motion under a constant force. Include units in mechanics answers.

questions.prompt: A biased coin has probability \(1/3\) of landing heads on each toss. Four tosses are independent. Find the probability of at least one head.
questions.hint: The complement of at least one head is no heads.
solution: The probability of a tail on one toss is \(2/3\). Independence means that the probability of four tails is \((2/3)^4=16/81\).
Therefore \(P(\text{at least one head})=1-16/81=65/81\).

questions.prompt: A data set has mean \(12\) and standard deviation \(3\). Every value \(x\) is replaced by \(y=2x-5\). Find the mean and standard deviation of the new data set.
questions.hint: A translation changes the centre but not the spread; multiplying every value scales the spread.
solution: The mean transforms in the same way as each value: \(\bar y=2\bar x-5=2(12)-5=19\).
Subtracting \(5\) does not change deviations from the mean. Multiplication by \(2\) doubles their sizes, so the standard deviation is \(2(3)=6\).

questions.topic: Newton's second law and constant acceleration
questions.prompt: A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) starts from rest on a smooth horizontal surface. A constant horizontal force of \(12\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on it. Find its displacement after \(4\,\mathrm{s}\).
questions.hint: Find the acceleration from the horizontal resultant force, then use a constant-acceleration equation.
solution: The surface is smooth, so there is no friction. Vertically, weight and the normal reaction balance. Horizontally, \(F=ma\) gives \(12=3a\), so \(a=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.answer: \(32\,\mathrm{m}\) in the direction of the force.

mistake.prompt: A particle has velocity \(v=(6-2t)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(0\leq t\leq5\), with \(t\) in seconds. A student finds a displacement of \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) and calls this the distance travelled. Find the actual distance.
mistake.hint: Locate the time at which the velocity changes sign, then add the distances on either side.
solution: The particle changes direction when \(6-2t=0\), at \(t=3\). Its displacement over the whole interval is indeed \([6t-t^2]_0^5=5\,\mathrm{m}\).
From \(0\) to \(3\) seconds it travels \([6t-t^2]_0^3=9\,\mathrm{m}\). From \(3\) to \(5\) seconds its displacement is \([6t-t^2]_3^5=-4\,\mathrm{m}\), so it travels a further \(4\,\mathrm{m}\).
Total distance is \(9+4=13\,\mathrm{m}\).

recommendations: Write down the random variable and modelling assumptions before calculating a binomial probability.
Predict how the mean and spread should change under coding before using a calculator.
For mechanics, start with a force diagram, a positive direction and a list of known quantities; check units at the end.

statistics-mechanics-year-2.title: Statistics and Mechanics Year 2
statistics-mechanics-year-2.intro: Three short checks on the normal distribution, projectiles and moments. A calculator may be used. Take gravitational acceleration as 9.8 metres per second squared.

questions.prompt: \(X\) is normally distributed with mean \(50\) and standard deviation \(4\). Find \(P(X>54)\), giving your answer to three significant figures.
questions.hint: Standardise using the standard deviation, then choose the upper tail.
solution: With \(Z=(X-50)/4\), the threshold \(X=54\) corresponds to \(Z=1\).
Hence \(P(X>54)=P(Z>1)=1-\Phi(1)\approx0.158655\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

questions.prompt: A particle is projected from level ground at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal. Neglect air resistance and take \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its time of flight and horizontal range when it returns to the same level.
questions.hint: Resolve the initial velocity into components. Use zero vertical displacement to find the non-zero flight time.
solution: The initial horizontal and vertical velocity components are \(20\cos30^\circ=10\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(20\sin30^\circ=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Taking upward as positive, vertical displacement is \(y=10t-4.9t^2\). At landing, \(y=0\); the non-zero solution is \(t=10/4.9=100/49\,\mathrm{s}\approx2.04\,\mathrm{s}\).
Horizontal velocity is constant, so the range is \((10\sqrt3)(100/49)=1000\sqrt3/49\,\mathrm{m}\approx35.3\,\mathrm{m}\).

questions.prompt: A uniform horizontal beam \(AB\) is \(4\,\mathrm{m}\) long and weighs \(40\,\mathrm{N}\). It is supported at \(A\) and \(B\). A further downward load of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) acts \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) from \(A\). Find the upward reactions at the two supports.
questions.hint: The beam's weight acts at its midpoint. Taking moments about one support eliminates its reaction.
solution: Let the upward reactions be \(R_A\) and \(R_B\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(R_A+R_B=40+20=60\,\mathrm{N}\).
Taking moments about \(A\), \(4R_B=40(2)+20(1)=100\). Therefore \(R_B=25\,\mathrm{N}\).
It follows that \(R_A=60-25=35\,\mathrm{N}\).

mistake.prompt: Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A)=0.4\), \(P(B)=0.5\) and \(P(A\cap B)=0.3\). A student writes \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)=0.4\). Explain why this is wrong and find the correct conditional probability.
mistake.hint: Conditioning on \(B\) changes the denominator. Independence must be established rather than assumed.
solution: The student's equality would hold for independent events. Here \(P(A)P(B)=0.4(0.5)=0.2\), which differs from \(P(A\cap B)=0.3\); the events are not independent.

recommendations: For normal probabilities, draw and shade the required tail before entering values; distinguish variance from standard deviation.
For projectiles, keep separate horizontal and vertical equations linked by the same time.
For equilibrium, draw every force at its point of application and choose a moment centre that removes an unknown.

core-pure-1.title: Core Pure Mathematics 1
core-pure-1.intro: Three short checks on complex numbers, matrices and proof by induction. In the proof, state why the induction step establishes the result for every positive integer.

questions.prompt: Solve \(z^2-4z+13=0\), giving both roots in the form \(a+bi\).
questions.hint: Complete the square and remember that \(i^2=-1\).
solution: Completing the square gives \((z-2)^2+9=0\), so \((z-2)^2=-9\).
Therefore \(z-2=\pm3i\), giving the conjugate roots \(2+3i\) and \(2-3i\).

questions.prompt: Find the inverse of \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), and use it to solve \(2x+y=7\), \(x+y=4\).
questions.hint: Calculate the determinant before applying the inverse formula for a two-by-two matrix.
solution: The determinant is \(2(1)-1(1)=1\), so \(M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\).

The equations are \(M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Premultiplying by \(M^{-1}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7-4\\-7+8\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Prove by induction that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+1)=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}3\) for every positive integer \(n\).
questions.hint: After assuming the formula for \(n=k\), add the next term \((k+1)(k+2)\) and factorise.
solution: For \(n=1\), the left side is \(1(2)=2\) and the right side is \(1(2)(3)/3=2\), so the statement is true.
Assume it is true for a positive integer \(k\): \(\sum_{r=1}^{k}r(r+1)=k(k+1)(k+2)/3\).
Then \[\begin{aligned}\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}r(r+1)&=\frac{k(k+1)(k+2)}3\\&\quad +(k+1)(k+2)\\&=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)}3.\end{aligned}\]
This is the required formula with \(n=k+1\). The statement holds at \(n=1\), and truth at any positive integer implies truth at the next; therefore it holds for every positive integer by induction.

mistake.prompt: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). A student assumes \(AB=BA\), as for ordinary numbers. Calculate both products to check the claim.
mistake.hint: Calculate entries using row-by-column multiplication; preserve the order of the matrices.
solution: \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), whereas \(BA=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
The top-right entries differ, so \(AB\neq BA\). Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general; factors cannot be reordered without justification.

recommendations: Check complex roots by substitution and use an Argand sketch to connect algebra with geometry.
When using matrices, preserve multiplication order and verify an inverse by multiplying back to the identity.
Write induction proofs with a base case, a clearly stated assumption, the next-step calculation and a conclusion.

core-pure-2.title: Core Pure Mathematics 2
core-pure-2.intro: Three short checks on complex roots, hyperbolic functions and differential equations. Give exact answers.

questions.prompt: Find all three complex roots of \(z^3=8\), in the form \(a+bi\).
questions.hint: Write \(8=8e^{2k\pi i}\), then take cube roots with three distinct arguments.
solution: The roots have modulus \(8^{1/3}=2\) and arguments \(2k\pi/3\), for \(k=0,1,2\).
Using \(z=2(\cos(2k\pi/3)+i\sin(2k\pi/3))\) gives \(2\), \(-1+i\sqrt3\) and \(-1-i\sqrt3\). These are distinct and account for all roots of the cubic.

questions.prompt: Solve \(\sinh x=3/4\) for real \(x\), giving an exact answer.
questions.hint: Use the exponential definition of \(\sinh x\), and set \(u=e^x>0\).
solution: Multiplying by \(2u\) gives \(2u^2-3u-2=0\), or \((2u+1)(u-2)=0\).
The root \(u=-1/2\) is impossible because \(e^x>0\). Thus \(u=2\), so \(x=\ln2\).

questions.hint: Find the two auxiliary roots, then use both initial conditions to determine the constants.
solution: The auxiliary equation is \(m^2-3m+2=(m-1)(m-2)=0\), giving distinct roots \(1\) and \(2\).
The general solution is \(y=Ae^x+Be^{2x}\), with \(y^{\prime}=Ae^x+2Be^{2x}\).
The initial conditions give \(A+B=1\) and \(A+2B=0\). Subtraction gives \(B=-1\), then \(A=2\). Hence \(y=2e^x-e^{2x}\).

mistake.prompt: The curve \(r=2\cos\theta\), for \(-\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi/2\), traces a circle once. A student calculates its enclosed area as \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta=4\). Identify the error and find the area.
mistake.hint: The polar area element is \(\tfrac12r^2\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). Use the double-angle identity for \(\cos^2\theta\).
solution: The student has integrated \(r\); the correct area formula is \(\tfrac12\int r^2\,\mathrm{d}\theta\).

Here the area is \[\begin{aligned}A&=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}4\cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\&=\left[\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\\&=\pi.\end{aligned}\]
As a check, multiplying the polar equation by \(r\) gives \(x^2+y^2=2x\), or \((x-1)^2+y^2=1\): a circle of radius \(1\), whose area is \(\pi\).

recommendations: For complex roots, organise modulus and argument separately and check that you have found the required number of distinct roots.
Derive unfamiliar hyperbolic identities from exponentials instead of transferring trigonometric signs from memory.
Check differential-equation solutions twice: substitute into the equation and then verify every initial or boundary condition.
